item.title: Chinese premier says China, Russia work side by side in complex, turbulent world
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 21:17:00
CHINA / DIPLOMACY Chinese premier says China, Russia work side by side in complex, turbulent world By Xinhua Published: Oct 21, 2026 09:17 PM
Chinese Premier Li Qiang said on Wednesday that China and Russia have in recent years stood side by side and moved forward together in the face of a complex and turbulent international landscape. Co-chairing the 31st regular meeting between Chinese and Russian heads of government with Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin in St. Petersburg, Li said that in recent years, under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, China and Russia have leveraged more dynamic and resilient cooperation to cushion the impact of external uncertainties and instability, and bilateral cooperation has continued to broaden and grow ever more steady. At present, he said, the China-Russia comprehensive strategic partnership of coordination for the new era is entering a new stage, marked by greater achievements and faster development. China stands ready to work with Russia in the spirit of mutual respect, mutual benefit and win-win cooperation to deepen and substantiate cooperation across various fields, better translate the important consensus reached by the two heads of state into concrete actions and tangible outcomes, better serve the development and revitalization of both countries, and bring greater benefits to the two peoples, Li said. Noting that this year marks the 25th anniversary of the signing of the Russia-China Treaty of Good-Neighborliness and Friendly Cooperation, Mishustin said the Russia-China comprehensive strategic partnership of coordination for a new era is currently at its highest level in history and has set an example for relations between countries. Despite uncertainties in the international landscape, Russia-China economic and trade cooperation has maintained sound momentum, he said. Russia is willing to work with China on the basis of mutual benefit, win-win cooperation, mutual respect and good-neighborliness and friendship, to further strengthen practical cooperation in various fields and safeguard the common interests of the two countries, he added. Li and Mishustin heard reports from representatives of both sides on the work of the China-Russia Investment Cooperation Committee, the China-Russia Energy Cooperation Committee, the China-Russia Committee on Humanities Cooperation, the committee for regular meetings between the Chinese and Russian heads of government, and the Intergovernmental Commission for Cooperation of Northeast China and the Far East Region of Russia. The two countries fully affirmed the work of the committees over the past year. Both sides agreed that strategic guidance from the heads of state is an important guarantee for the steady development of China-Russia relations. China and Russia should take the important consensus of the two heads of state as the fundamental guide, advance cooperation in key areas such as economy and trade, investment, energy and resources, connectivity, aerospace, finance and industry, foster new drivers of development in frontier areas such as artificial intelligence, biotechnology and the digital economy, jointly ensure the success of the China-Russia Years of Education, strengthen people-to-people and cultural exchanges in tourism, culture, youth and media, stimulate the vitality of local cooperation, maintain close communication and coordination on multilateral affairs, and strive for more practical outcomes. After the meeting, Li and Mishustin signed the joint communique of the 31st regular meeting between Chinese and Russian heads of government. The two sides also reached cooperation documents in areas such as economy and trade, space, science and technology, and education.

item.title: China's cumulative carbon emission trading volume exceeds 1 billion tonnes; country offers insights for global action addressing climate change
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 21:13:00
An aerial drone photo taken on June 3, 2026 shows a farming-photovoltaic power complementary project in Huimin County, Binzhou City, East China's Shandong Province. Photo: VCG China has established the world's largest carbon emissions trading market, with cumulative trading volume in its national carbon emissions trading market surpassing one billion tonnes, an official from the Ministry of Ecology and Environment said on Wednesday, highlighting it as one of China's key achievements in tackling climate change. The figures were released at a press conference on Wednesday ahead of the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), which will be held in Antalya, Turkey, from November 9 to 20. A Chinese expert said China's sustained efforts in climate action can offer valuable experience for other countries. In just over five years, China has established the world's largest carbon emissions trading market, covering about 8.3 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide, or more than 65 percent of the country's total emissions , said Li Gao, vice minister of ecology and environment, during the press conference held by the State Council Information Office, per Xinhua. In terms of emissions reduction and efficiency gains, China helped reduce carbon dioxide emissions from the thermal power sector by approximately 530 million tonnes during the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-25). Internationally, China's carbon market has received widespread recognition for its achievements and has become an important platform for showcasing the country's efforts to address climate change, the CCTV report said. During the same conference, Li also said that China will send a delegation to attend COP31 and will actively advance international climate negotiations. COP31 will conduct negotiations and consultations on nearly 100 agenda items related to the implementation of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, covering mitigation, adaptation, finance and just transition, per CCTV News. "As a responsible major developing country, China has consistently participated in and advanced international climate negotiations in a proactive and constructive manner," Li said, adding that China will contribute Chinese wisdom, solutions and strength to the success of COP31. Ma Jun, director of the Institute of Public and Environmental Affairs, told the Global Times that the gap between emission reduction pledges and real action remains wide, with current global efforts falling short of global climate targets and climate overshoot increasingly unavoidable. Geopolitical divisions fragment global governance, hinder climate cooperation and complicate efforts to balance energy, food and climate security, he noted. Some developing countries also struggle to balance climate mitigation and adaptation with economic growth and poverty alleviation, constrained by severe shortages of finance, technology and capacity, Ma added. The expert noted that China's sustained climate action offers a valuable lesson by integrating emissions reduction with pollution control and green transformation. Linking clean energy, energy-efficiency upgrades and electric vehicles with environmental improvement, resource recycling, industrial upgrading and job creation can address climate change while creating new sources of green growth. Through South-South cooperation, China can help other developing countries strengthen their capacity for independent climate action and reduce transition costs by sharing appropriate technologies, project experience and training. These lessons should, of course, be adapted to each country's resource endowments and stage of development, Ma noted. Li said during the press conference on Wednesday that China has built the world's largest and most complete clean energy industrial chain, with green and low-carbon industries becoming an important engine of economic growth, according to a report by the Xinhua News Agency. By the first half of 2026, the country's total installed renewable energy capacity reached 2.46 billion kilowatts, accounting for 60.7 percent of total national power generation capacity. At the end of July, installed solar power capacity surpassed coal power for the first time in history, making it China's largest single power source. Moreover, China's combined installed capacity of operational and approved nuclear power units has risen to first place in the world. New energy vehicle production and sales have ranked first globally for 11 consecutive years. On Wednesday, the Ministry of Ecology and Environment also released an annual report on China's policies and actions for addressing climate change 2026, outlining China's basic position and proposals for the COP31. "China will continue to play a proactive and constructive role, support Turkey in its capacity as the COP31 Presidency and Australia as the President of Negotiations, and work with other Parties in the spirit of a community with a shared future for humanity to ensure that COP31 focuses on implementation and cooperation," it reads.

item.title: China unveils insurance sector development roadmap during 2026-2030 at Financial Street Forum
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 21:06:00
Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum (FSF) 2026 in Beijing on October 20, 2026 Photo: Yin Yeping/GT China's insurance industry has outlined three major priorities for high-quality development during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) to support economic and social development, deepen reform and opening-up, and strengthen risk prevention, according to a research report released at the Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum 2026 in Beijing. The report, titled Research on High-Quality Development of the Insurance Industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period, was released by Zhao Yulong, president of the Insurance Association of China, at the forum's first-ever insurance conference, which opened on Tuesday, according to a Xinhua News Agency report on Wednesday. The research identifies three core tasks for the industry. The first is to better serve economic and social development by strengthening insurance support for new quality productive forces, improving social governance and enhancing people's livelihood protection. The second focuses on deepening reform and opening-up, including improving the insurance market system, advancing reforms in key areas, accelerating digital transformation and further opening the sector to foreign participation. The third is to strengthen risk prevention and control. Zhao said the research addresses major national strategies, priority areas and weaknesses in economic and social development during the 15th Five-Year Plan, while proposing targeted solutions to shortcomings identified during the previous five-year period. The report also proposes 18 indicators to assess the industry's high-quality development, reflecting a shift from pursuing rapid expansion and scale toward prioritizing quality and efficiency. Looking ahead, the research outlines a three-stage development roadmap for the insurance sector. The first stage, covering 2026 to 2030, focuses on strengthening the industry's foundations, including market development, risk management, supply capacity and opening-up. The second stage, from 2031 to 2035, emphasizes improving quality and efficiency, while the third, from 2036 to 2050, aims to establish insurance as a key pillar of China's development into a financial powerhouse. Zhao said the research also reviewed the industry's achievements during the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), including improvements in institutional frameworks, services to the real economy and public welfare. However, challenges remain, including insufficient insurance coverage, gaps between products and market needs, and uneven development. The research project, led by the Insurance Association of China, involved more than 150 experts from over 30 insurance institutions and took six months to complete. The association will refine the report before publishing it and organizing industry discussions to support the implementation of China's 15th Five-Year Plan and its financial development objectives, Zhao said. The insurance conference, held for the first time as part of the Financial Street Forum, features discussions on technology insurance, inclusive insurance, pension insurance and disaster insurance. It is expected to release additional research findings and case studies aimed at promoting higher-quality development and greater opening-up of the sector. Global Times

item.title: China permits, monitors Philippine resupply to illegally grounded vessel at Ren'ai Jiao: CCG spokesperson
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 20:21:00
File photo of a China Coast Guard (CCG) ship in the South China Sea Photo: VCG With approval from the Chinese side, the Philippines delivered living necessities to its ship illegally "grounded" at China's Ren'ai Jiao on Wednesday, China Coast Guard (CCG) spokesperson Jiang Lue said, according to a statement from the CCG on Wednesday. The CCG inquired and verified the Philippine vessel conducting the delivery, and monitored the whole process. The CCG will continue to conduct law-enforcement and rights-protection operations in China's Nansha Qundao and its adjacent waters, including Ren'ai Jiao, in accordance with the law, the statement said. item.title: It is not that storms bypass China, but that we have built a steady shield: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20 23:51:00
Bustling scenes on Nanjing Road, East China's Shanghai Municipality on September 14, 2023 Photo: VCG This autumn of 2026 lays bare a stark contrast between a turbulent world and China's stable governance. On one side, the ongoing conflict in the Middle East keeps roiling global energy supplies. Diesel prices in Europe and the US have climbed to an all time high of around $220 per barrel. Meanwhile, France and wider Europe are gripped by sustained unrest, with long simmering social contradictions boiling over. On the other side, China presents a vastly different picture over the same period. Nationwide cross regional trips reached 2.144 billion over the seven day National Day holiday, bringing the combined figure for the Mid Autumn and National Day holidays close to 2.8 billion as people traveled across the country. In September, China's consumer price index (CPI) rose by just 0.9 percent year on year, while food prices actually fell by 1.7 percent. The world is in turmoil, yet ordinary Chinese people can still plan trips and live their lives with peace of mind. Many are asking why the global crises unfolding elsewhere seem to have limited impact on China. The answer is straightforward: It's not that the storm has automatically veered off course; it's that we have preemptively shielded people's livelihoods from these risks. Ample, diversified stockpiles form the first "flood retention zone" that stabilizes prices, preventing violent swings in international markets from spilling over into households' grocery baskets and store shelves. As the world's largest crude oil importer, China's crude imports tumbled to roughly 8.1 million barrels per day in the second quarter. Imports fell below 8 million barrels per day in May and June, hitting the lowest level since 2016. Even so, there was no shortage of refined oil supply domestically. Industry estimates that China's strategic petroleum reserves are ample. Together with substantial inventories of refined products, these reserves provide a reliable buffer at the onset of a crisis. Where others face immediate supply collapse once shipments are cut off, China holds sufficient reserves to stay calm. At the same time, the bottom line of China's food security remains firmly secured. Summer grain output in 2026 surpassed 300 billion jin (150 million tonnes) for the first time. The country's daily capacity to process and supply grain and edible oils exceeds 1.8 million tons for each category. These national stockpiles grant China ample room for maneuver amid external shocks. A complete and highly resilient industrial chain acts as a "wave breaking dyke" that dampens the transmission of risks. Shocks from rising global commodity prices are absorbed and softened at successive links along the industrial chain, so their impact on end consumer goods is greatly diluted by the time they reach shoppers. To be clear, China is not immune to external shocks - as reflected in that 32 percent quarter on quarter drop in crude imports in Q2. But production never ground to a halt. In September, the value added output of industrial enterprises above designated size rose 5.5 percent year on year, with a 5.3 percent cumulative gain for the first three quarters. Manufacturing output grew 6.0 percent, automobile manufacturing by 6.7 percent, and electronics manufacturing surged by 16.4 percent. While fierce storms rage abroad, our factories keep running and industrial links hold firm. That is our source of confidence. Behind this lies the resilience provided by China's diversified energy system. In the first nine months of this year, domestic output of raw coal from industrial enterprises above designated size reached 3.45 billion tons, crude oil 164.6 million tons, and natural gas 196.7 billion cubic meters. In September, nuclear, wind and solar power generation increased by 21.5 percent, 10.6 percent and 19.5 percent year-on-year, respectively. By the end of August, installed photovoltaic capacity surpassed that of coal-fired power for the first time in history, becoming China's largest source of installed power generation capacity. When the price of one energy source rises, alternative sources can quickly step in to fill the gap. More importantly, China's industrial chains have mechanisms for absorbing and sharing costs, meaning that rising raw material prices are not simply passed directly on to consumers. In September, national industrial producer purchase prices rose 6.9 percent year-on-year, while prices in upstream coal mining surged 35.3 percent and those in oil and gas extraction climbed 24.5 percent year-on-year. By proactively reducing profit margins and flexibly adjusting production schedules, the domestic refining and petrochemical sector, in conjunction with the refined oil price regulation mechanism, ultimately limited the year-over-year increase in domestic retail prices for refined oil products to 16.6 percent. In some other countries, the surge in global oil prices has translated directly into higher household expenses. Why is China consistently able to build a solid bulwark against turbulent winds and rough seas? The answer lies in an efficient, well-coordinated and proactive government that takes a holistic approach and intervenes when necessary to provide timely support. Ahead of the summer peak in energy demand, the government made early arrangements to ensure energy supplies nationwide. A high proportion of medium- and long-term contracts for thermal coal, electricity and natural gas were signed and fulfilled, laying a solid foundation for stable supplies and prices. This summer, China's national peak electricity demand set new records three times, reaching a high of 1.553 billion kilowatts. Yet coal inventories at centrally dispatched power plants consistently remained sufficient for more than 30 days of consumption. Not a single province experienced power rationing, and no region had to implement rolling blackout. Faced with a massive travel surge totaling 2.144 billion passenger trips during China's National Day holiday, public security, transportation and meteorological authorities worked in coordination to support road travel, with self-driving trips accounting for more than 90 percent of journeys. Travel by new-energy vehicles reached 1.8 times the usual daily level, while expressways continued to operate smoothly even as traffic peaked at 71 million vehicles on the first day of the holidays. It is precisely the combination of an efficient market and a proactive government that ensures economic and social activities can be effectively organized and coordinated. Looking ahead, global turbulence will not easily disappear, and new "gray rhino" and "black swan" events could emerge at any moment. China has never been sheltered from the storms sweeping the world. What makes a major country truly great is not merely its vast size or its loud voice, but its ability to ensure that, even amid raging storms, ordinary people can still buy their daily groceries, turn on the lights and begin another ordinary day with peace of mind. Those 2.144 billion passenger trips represent more than just a travel boom. They are also a confident testament to the country's chosen path of development. It is not that the storms have passed China by, but that China has kept their full force from disrupting the everyday lives of hundreds of millions of people.

item.title: GT Voice: What's the meaning of deeper China-Europe vehicle bonds?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20 23:44:00
China EU relations The global new-energy vehicle (NEV) wave is driving a profound transformation in Europe's automotive industry, one driven by market realities and development needs rather than political noise. One of its most striking features is the unprecedented deepening of the bonds between Europe's auto sector and China's NEV supply chain. Following the official inauguration of Leapmotor B10 production last week, Leapmotor International plans to produce the Leapmotor B05, its second model at the Stellantis manufacturing plant in Zaragoza, Spain, Stellantis announced on its official website on Monday. Meanwhile, Volkswagen is evaluating bringing some of its China-only models to Europe, and is starting to export to the Global South and countries that have easier access from China than Europe, such as Australia and the Middle East, Volkswagen CEO Thomas Schäfer told Autocar at the Paris motor show. While these two news items appear to involve different companies and different operational segments, they point to a shared phenomenon against the backdrop of Europe's electric transition: Chinese and European automotive supply chains are integrating far more deeply than expected. Rather than being swayed by political rhetoric, European carmakers have made choices consistent with commercial logic through orders, factories, and export routes. What makes this phenomenon particularly notable is its sharp contrast with the narrative that some European politicians have been hyping. For some time, there has been no shortage of rhetoric surrounding China-Europe electric vehicle (EV) competition, with certain political forces and extreme voices reducing normal industrial collaboration to a zero-sum game and even pushing protectionist measures. Yet European automakers on the front lines of the transition have chosen to actively deepen ties with China's new-energy supply chain in a thoroughly market-driven way, offering the industry's own response through concrete production arrangements and product launches. The fundamental driver behind this pragmatic choice is the enormous cost and technology pressure brought by the electric transition. According to a report from the Boston Consulting Group, average vehicle plant utilization across European original equipment manufacturers is roughly 60 percent, compared with the 80 percent benchmark. European automakers also need to invest heavily annually in EV research and development and production line upgrades. This heavy burden has left European vehicle plants operating under pressure. If European manufacturers were to rely solely on domestic resources to fill gaps in batteries, electrical and electronic architectures, and intelligent vehicle platforms, the process would take a lot of time and costs would escalate. It is under these very real constraints that European automakers have taken the initiative to seek out high-quality partners globally. Chinese power battery companies now hold impressive global market share, and the country's proven capabilities in full-vehicle development iteration speed, supply chain coordination efficiency and cost control have created comparative advantages that cannot be replicated in the short term. They have naturally become the partners that European automakers turn to. This level of industrial alignment is a rational decision made based on market logic rather than political narrative. This deepening integration also signals a new phase of global EV competition, one in which competition is no longer simply about whose technology is more sophisticated, but about supply chain integration capability. European automakers have deep foundations in brands, channels, and manufacturing standards, while China's supply chain offers unique advantages in batteries, electrical and electronic architectures, iteration speed, and cost control. Each side has its shortcomings when going it alone; together, they may produce more competitive products. More importantly, the nature of China-Europe vehicle ties is undergoing a shift, with each side becoming an indispensable link in the other's supply chain. With global protectionism on the rise, businesses will find the most efficient solutions in their own ways, even amid mounting pressure and noise. This is perhaps the truest aspect of China-Europe vehicle relations, and the core logic behind European carmakers' pragmatic choices: whoever chooses pragmatic solutions sooner will seize the initiative in the electric transition.

item.title: Visa-free foreign entries rise 24.1% in Q3 as 'China Haul' reflects appeal of Chinese innovation, experiences
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20 23:04:00
Foreign tourists visit the Central Street in Harbin, northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, July 22, 2026. Thanks to the visa-free entry policies, China has witnessed an increasing number of foreign tourists visiting China this summer. According to the official data, 77.7 percent of foreign visitors entering China in the first half of the year enjoyed visa-free entry policies. (Xinhua/Na Yuqi) "So that's six phones in total, right?" A buyer from Kazakhstan attending the Canton Fair told the Global Times that she was calling family and friends while shopping at a mall to tally their requests. "At the moment, I plan to buy six phones. I'm still counting how many earphones, AI glasses and smart toothbrushes I need. so far, I need to buy more than10 earphones and more than 10 smart wristbands." Her expanding shopping list offers a glimpse of the consumer activity surrounding China's growing appeal to international visitors. Foreign nationals made 8.992 million visa-free entries into China in the third quarter of 2026, up 24.1 percent year-on-year and accounting for 77.5 percent of foreign entries, the National Immigration Administration (NIA) said on Tuesday. Total entries by foreign nationals reached 11.601 million, up 15.6 percent year-on-year. Following the popularity of "China Travel" and "Chinamaxxing," a trend embracing aspects of Chinese daily life, "China Haul" is gaining traction on overseas social media, with visitors sharing shopping finds. Experts said easier entry procedures and the emergence of innovative products were encouraging foreign visitors to gain a deeper understanding of and experience China. Jiang Yiyi, dean of the School of Leisure Sports and Tourism at Beijing Sport University, told the Global Times on Tuesday that the continued expansion of visa-free arrangements, improved border clearance services and convenient transportation were jointly supporting growth in inbound travel. Zhang Yi, CEO and chief analyst at iiMedia Research, said visitors' interest in innovative products reflected recognition of China's technological progress. Their recommendations and posts shared overseas could further amplify that recognition and encourage businesses to continuously improve their product offerings. The trend brings together two sources of appeal: products reflecting technological advances and everyday goods offering variety and value. For businesses, the opportunity extends from purchases made during a visit to recommendations that introduce those products to consumers in other countries, said observers. From electronics to accessories, overseas consumers are finding products that combine practical functions, distinctive designs and affordable prices. Shakhzod Mirzaev Richard, an Uzbekistani student in Hangzhou, East China's Zhejiang Province, bought electronics, clothes and small gifts for family and friends back home during his several years of living and studying in China. His friends also purchased gadgets and accessories to take home. "China offers many choices at reasonable prices. You can find useful, good-quality products without spending too much," he told the Global Times. Families and friends in Uzbekistan were often curious about Chinese products, especially new technology, he said. For him, trying products firsthand helps explain their appeal. Recalling a recent VR game, he said: "For a moment, I almost forgot I was playing a game." Such experiences show how advanced technology has become and help explain the interest in AI glasses and drones, he added. "They are not just interesting to look at; people can actually try them and experience what they can do." A merchant selling smart electronics in Yiwu, East China's Zhejiang, told the Global Times that the number of foreign visitors had noticeably increased since September, with electrical appliances and AI-powered products attracting interest. In Shanghai, Australian visitor Wayne traveled to the city after attending the Canton Fair. He said China's visa-free entry policy for Australians had made border clearance smooth. His purchases included Disney- and Ultraman-themed trading cards. "This trading card game is really popular back home in Australia," he said. Maria, a Brazilian visitor, selected phone straps, bag charms and five blind boxes for family and friends. She discovered blind boxes on TikTok and said such novelty goods were available only online in Brazil. "The designs are so lovely and unique - we do not have styles like these in Brazil, and similar accessories are extremely pricey there," she said. A comparable phone charm could cost more than 200 yuan in Brazil, against 20 to 30 yuan in China. These experiences reflect a broader trend in inbound tourism. Russia, South Korea and Vietnam were the top three source countries for foreign visitors to China in the third quarter, while the top 10 source countries accounted for 63.9 percent of all foreign arrivals, according to the NIA. Citing Trip.com data, Xinhua's Globe magazine reported that summer bookings by Brazilian travelers rose 358.52 percent year-on-year, while those by Swiss travelers increased 234.73 percent. Zhangjiajie climbed from 13th to seventh place among Chinese cities receiving inbound travelers on the platform. The summer travel trend also extended beyond shopping. Globe magazine reported growing interest in destinations offering cooler weather and smaller cities, where travelers can explore natural landscapes and local cultures. The growing diversity of travel experiences is giving foreign visitors more reasons to venture beyond major international gateway cities and discover more of China. Jiang said lesser-known destinations, food experiences and interactive cultural activities were enriching China's tourism offerings, while high-speed rail and new-energy vehicles had themselves become attractions. "Shopping is also a very important part of the overall tourism experience," she said. Richard said many foreigners are discovering a China more modern and technologically advanced than they had expected. After seeing products on social media, people wanted to try and buy them, linking online curiosity with purchases and experiences during their visits. The Uzbekistani student described "China Haul" as a natural next step in a trend driven by social media, which encourages people to try products for themselves. "For me, 'China Haul' is not just about shopping; it's also about discovering new things and taking a little piece of the China experience back home." China has continued to expand its visa-free entry arrangements and improve shopping services this year. On August 20, Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam were added to the list of countries eligible for China's 240-hour visa-free transit policy and Hainan's 30-day visa-free entry policy, bringing the total number of eligible countries to 57 and 61, respectively. Jiang attributed the growth in inbound travel to policy improvements, better transport connections and a wider range of tourism products. The restoration and expansion of direct flights, cross-border railways and other transport links were making travel to China more convenient, she said. A notice issued by six government departments in May introduced further improvements to departure tax refunds. From July 1, refund applications involving sales of less than 10,000 yuan became subject to random physical inspections, while applications involving sales of 10,000 yuan or more remained subject to individual inspections. The measures also enabled paperless processing throughout the refund process. The notice also promoted cross-regional recognition of "instant refund" services, allowing travelers receiving an advance refund in one location to complete departure tax refund procedures at another eligible port. It also standardized the departure deadline for the service at 28 days. Payment and delivery services are also adapting to the needs of international visitors. For example, Chinese e-commerce giant JD.com said in July that eligible travelers shopping in Beijing could use its Chinese- or English-language interface of its app, link overseas bank cards and submit tax refund information online. Purchases could be delivered to hotels or designated addresses within Beijing. The measures address successive stages of a visitor's journey, from entering China to paying for purchases and arranging delivery. Combined with product innovation, these practical improvements help explain why shopping is becoming a more prominent part of international visitors' experiences in China, experts noted. Official figures reflect the growing scale of tax-refund shopping. In the first half of 2026, the number of overseas travelers obtaining departure tax refunds increased 366 percent year-on-year, while sales of eligible goods and the total value of refunds both grew 69 percent, according to the State Taxation Administration. Jiang said product variety of products, competitive prices and improved shopping environment were encouraging overseas visitors to spend. Zhang also noted that greater recognition of Chinese innovation, amplified through overseas social media, could create a positive cycle supporting further innovation. As China continues to open up, visitors' purchases and experiences are also creating opportunities to share the country's development achievements with the world. Continued innovation would further strengthen China's capabilities and provide "better products for people around the world to enjoy," Zhang said.

item.title: Washington issues penalty tickets in vain while staring at DeepSeek's taillights: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20 21:44:00
Illustration: Liu Rui/GT America's absurd ban has done nothing to slow the progress of China's large language models. The harder Washington clamps down, the more it lays bare its anxiety and powerlessness in the face of China's AI rise. In the end, Washington has issued piles of punitive orders yet cannot even catch a glimpse of DeepSeek's taillights. On October 19 local time, the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued an official notice, ordering all federal civilian agencies to remove products developed by Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd (DeepSeek), and its affiliated entities from their IT systems, and prohibiting the procurement and use of third-party products and services built on DeepSeek technology. Yet just two days before the ban was unveiled, DeepSeek's new model V4.1-Flash-1017 claimed the top spot among open-source models on Code Arena: WebDev, scoring 1,670 points to outperform closed-source models including America's Claude Opus 5 and Grok 4.7. The irony could not be sharper. A close look at DHS's list of accusations reveals nothing but speculative language: DeepSeek "may result in the transfer of sensitive data" to China, the model could pose "multiple threat vectors." Every charge relies on "may", "might" and "concerns," without a single shred of hard evidence. Washington politicians have long mastered this tactic of levelling charges on flimsy grounds. When Huawei built a competitive 5G network, it was labelled a "security threat." When TikTok won hundreds of millions of US users, it was smeared as a "surveillance tool." Now that DeepSeek has built an R1-class model with a training cost of roughly $6 million, matching the performance of OpenAI's models built with hundreds of millions of dollars in investment and shaking up the global market, accusations of "knowledge distillation" soon followed. In reality, DeepSeek has never been found to pose any of the risks mentioned in the aforementioned announcements. By contrast, multiple US tech products have repeatedly been caught red-handed with "backdoor" surveillance and data breaches, which makes this DHS notice reads more like a "brutal self-satire" of Washington. Many observers have noticed the notice bears a July 24 date, meaning the ban has been in place for nearly three months. Over those three months, DeepSeek has made steady leaps in reasoning, coding, agentic capabilities and cost control. It first narrowed the performance gap with top US models, and soon outpaced them. Viewed in hindsight, this upward trajectory is a stark mockery of Washington. Its absurd ban has done nothing to slow the progress of China's large language models. The harder Washington clamps down, the more it lays bare its anxiety and powerlessness in the face of China's AI rise. In the end, Washington has issued piles of punitive orders yet cannot even catch a glimpse of DeepSeek's taillights - and the crackdown has inadvertently given DeepSeek free publicity. This absurd contrast stems fundamentally from the collision of two development paths on the AI track: "closed-off containment" versus "open-source breakout." From its inception, DeepSeek has stuck to an open development model. It releases core model weights to global developers, fully opens its toolchains and technical documentation, and subjects all performance and security features to worldwide public scrutiny. US tech giants, by contrast, have long followed a closed-source monopolistic approach. Their black-box technology is itself the biggest source of cybersecurity risks. Now Washington is trying to block an open, transparent open-source ecosystem in the name of national security, and the logical contradiction could not be more obvious. What truly worries Washington is the remarkable speed at which China is visibly catching up in artificial intelligence. Yet the increasingly stringent restrictions are undermining America's own innovation ecosystem. The bans target not only DeepSeek itself but also third-party products that use its technology. Legislation being advanced in Congress goes even further, prohibiting American companies from selling software developed on the basis of Chinese AI models to the government. The reality, however, is that American companies such as Snowflake and Vercel have already integrated DeepSeek technology into their products. Following the release of its new model, discussions on overseas social media platforms generated hundreds of thousands of posts. Even an AI adviser to the Trump administration has acknowledged that AI companies should not seek administrative protections to shield themselves from competition. Keeping the most dynamic technologies out of the country is tantamount to locking up the toolboxes of America's own developers. From algorithm optimization under chip restrictions to ecosystem adaptation for domestic computing platforms and breakthroughs in indigenous AI chip development, Chinese technology companies have long grown accustomed to forging ahead under pressure. DeepSeek's open-source strategy is precisely the most powerful response to technological blockades: If you close the door, we will open ours even wider, allowing developers around the world to use the technology for free and improve it together. As developers and small and medium-sized enterprises in more countries gain access to AI models comparable to the world's best at extremely low cost, the benefits of technological diffusion will draw an increasing number of participants toward an open ecosystem. The isolationism of unilateral technological blockades will inevitably find itself isolated by a global consensus in favor of technological openness. China and the US each have their own strengths in AI and should work together through dialogue and cooperation to manage risks and share the benefits. The two countries' leaders have already established a dialogue mechanism on AI issues, setting the broad direction for cooperation. Yet Washington's contradictory approach of talking about cooperation while simultaneously imposing bans will only erode the foundation of mutual trust. It is hoped that Washington will fully and faithfully implement the consensus reached by the two heads of state. This would benefit not only China and the US, but also the world as a whole.
